A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work on task representation shift in context-based offline meta reinforcement learning. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, and appendices support comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark learning curves, update-frequency and integration experiments, and training-time measurements.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments across encoder objectives and update schedules, data-quality tests, pretraining comparisons, and representation visualizations.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes from RETRO's fixed every-other-step cross-entropy update to a general framework with conditional encoder updates and a repeated-update loop bounded by accumulated representation shift. Section 4.3 instantiates different update and accumulation settings across three objectives. The classifier loss and BRAC policy backbone remain.

E1.justification: Point-Robot and Humanoid-Dir are removed from evaluation; Ant-Dir, Reach, Button-Press, and Dial-Turn remain. Section 5.3 adds separately collected random, medium, and expert Ant-Dir datasets, extending coverage to different behavior-policy data distributions.

E2.justification: v1 compares RETRO against UNICORN, FOCAL, CSRO, and Classifier. v2 instead compares update schedules within three objectives. Appendix 8.3 identifies FOCAL and the classifier implementation behind the contrastive and cross-entropy labels, so these are not entirely new comparators. CSRO disappears from evaluation, tuned UNICORN is replaced by reconstruction-only UNICORN-0, and pretrained encoders become additional comparison conditions.

E3.justification: Appendix Table 1 changes the reported learning rate from 4e-3 to 3e-4, while the main learning curves extend from 200,000 to 300,000 steps. v2 introduces frozen-encoder pretraining controls and a broader objective-by-schedule evaluation design. The 20 training and 20 testing task counts, shared network sizes, and retained benchmarks' dataset sizes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's frequency and method-integration studies are reworked into broader schedule comparisons across encoder objectives. v2 adds data-quality robustness tests, pretraining versus alternating-training comparisons, and a t-SNE case study relating task separation to returns. The training-time comparison is removed.

E5.justification: v1's learning-curve captions report four random seeds; v2's corresponding experimental reporting specifies eight seeds per configuration. Both versions show means with standard-deviation shading. No confidence intervals or formal significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: The six-benchmark baseline curves and timing results are replaced by objective-and-schedule results. New findings include contrastive learning failing on random Ant-Dir data, pretrained frozen encoders obtaining lower returns than alternating training, and weaker visual task separation accompanying higher returns in selected examples. Changed learning rates and training horizons prevent interpreting the replacement curves as same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: The central return and performance-difference bounds remain, but v1's empirical-distribution Corollary 4.11 is replaced by training-process Theorem 4.10, with a new approximation-error assumption, sample bound, and proof. v2 also adds the pretraining Corollary 6.1 and proofs for both background lemmas. Separately, Theorem 3.1 drops v1's explicit I(Z; M; X_b) >= 0 premise.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion drop the central claims of a named, tuning-free, one-line RETRO algorithm achieving SOTA performance, stability, and training-time advantages. v2 instead emphasizes identifying representation shift and demonstrating benefits from appropriate encoder updates across objectives and data qualities. The connection to expected-return optimization remains central.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations about delaying encoder updates while policy improvements accumulate, frozen pretrained representations restricting optimization freedom, and t-SNE separation being insufficient to predict returns. Section 6.1 newly argues that nonzero pretrained-representation error prevents monotonic improvement. v1's preference for a tuning-free half-frequency schedule and its slower-initial-convergence caveat disappear.

D1.justification: Appendix 8.3 identifies UNICORN-0 as the reconstruction implementation while retaining FOCAL code provenance and the classifier construction. Prior baseline hyperparameter-search grids, the CSRO code link, and RTX3090/concurrent-run hardware details are removed. The learning-rate entry changes, but most shared architecture, batch-size, and context details remain.

R1.justification: Most related work remains. v2 adds ContrBAR and contrasts its method-specific guarantee with the paper's claimed broader applicability, adds a safe-RL citation, and removes the Sutton and Barto reference. It also more explicitly distinguishes improving a given encoder's training process from designing a better representation objective.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, practical-method description, experimental narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the revised contribution. The RETRO-centered experimental subsections are replaced by main-results and data-quality sections, followed by a new Discussion section. This substantially changes the narrative structure beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 adds a training-framework schematic and replaces the earlier baseline, integration, frequency, and timing displays with objective-by-benchmark grids, data-quality grids, pretraining curves, and t-SNE plots. Plot legends and training-step axes change. The parameter tables move to a separate appendix page, and Table 2 loses two environment columns.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens investigation of update schedules through broader controls, data-quality tests, eight-seed reporting, and expanded derivations. However, it reduces benchmark coverage and implementation detail, drops Theorem 3.1's stated premise, and introduces an overstrong pretraining interpretation: Section 6.1 rules out monotonic improvement for nonzero representation error, although Corollary 6.1 permits errors below a positive threshold. These substantive gains and weaknesses leave the net quality change uncertain.
